text:
The Dark Side of the Moon

On April 11, 1970, Apollo 13 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center at 2:13 in the afternoon, Houston time. It carried three men: James Lovell, the commander, who had already flown to the Moon once, on Apollo 8; Jack Swigert, a late replacement who had joined the crew only days before; and Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, who was to walk on the Moon's Fra Mauro highlands. Swigert was there because the original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and was grounded. The launch was nearly flawless. The center engine of the second stage shut down early, but the others burned longer to compensate, and the crew reached orbit with no more than a ripple of concern. Public interest was thin. Two Moon landings had already been accomplished, and the networks had passed on broadcasting the crew's television transmissions.

For two days, the flight was routine. The crew docked with the lunar module, which they had named Aquarius, pulled it free of its launch adapter, and settled into the long coast toward the Moon. The command and service module was called Odyssey. On the evening of April 13, some 200,000 miles from home, Houston asked the crew to stir the oxygen and hydrogen tanks in the service module, a routine procedure meant to keep the supercold contents from stratifying. Swigert flipped the switch. Ninety-odd seconds later, there was a bang.

It was not a large noise, and Lovell at first thought Haise had played a prank with the lunar module's pressure relief valve. Then the instruments began to disagree with the world. A main electrical bus lost voltage. Thrusters fired on their own. Lovell, looking out of a window, saw gas streaming into space, and he said the words that became famous in a slightly altered form: "Houston, we've had a problem." Oxygen tank number two had burst. The explosion had also damaged tank number one, and within about three hours it too was empty. The command module's fuel cells, which needed oxygen to make electricity and water, were dying.

The cause lay years in the past. The tank's heating elements had been designed for 28 volts, but the launch pad ran on 65. During a ground test, the thermostat switches had welded shut, and the heaters had baked the tank's interior for hours, melting the Teflon insulation on the wires. Nobody had noticed. When Swigert flipped his switch, a spark leapt from a bare wire into oxygen under high pressure, and the tank, in effect, became a bomb.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz and his controllers worked through the first hours in a dense fog of ambiguous data. The Moon landing was abandoned almost at once; the only question was whether the crew could be brought home alive. Odyssey had perhaps a few hours of power left. The lunar module, however, was a self-contained spacecraft, designed to keep two men alive for two days on the surface. The plan was to use it as a lifeboat. Lovell and Haise crawled into Aquarius, and Swigert followed, powering down Odyssey so that its dwindling batteries could be saved for reentry.

Then came the matter of the route. The spacecraft was on a path that would loop around the Moon and miss Earth by a wide margin, and the service module's main engine could no longer be trusted. Controllers chose to use the lunar module's descent engine for a burn that would put the ship on a trajectory to swing around the Moon and return. A later burn, two hours after closest approach, sped up the return by about ten hours. Lovell, Haise, and Swigert passed behind the Moon and saw its far side, 158 miles below, in silence and with no radio contact. They had no time to appreciate it. When they emerged, the real struggle began.

Aquarius was built for two men and two days. Now it had to support three men for four. Power was the first problem; the crew shut down nearly everything, and the cabin temperature sank toward 38 degrees Fahrenheit. Water was the second. Rationed to a few ounces each per day, the men grew dehydrated, and Haise developed a kidney infection and a fever. Condensation ran down the walls. Sleep was nearly impossible in the cold, and the men took turns trying to doze in the command module's tunnel or in whatever corner offered a little warmth.

The third problem was the most insidious. Every breath adds carbon dioxide to the cabin, and the lunar module's lithium hydroxide canisters, which scrub it from the air, were designed for two people. As the gas level climbed toward the danger zone, the canisters filled. Odyssey had plenty of canisters, but they were square, and Aquarius's receptacles were round. On the ground, engineers dumped onto a table the very objects the crew had on board: cardboard, plastic bags, suit hoses, duct tape. They improvised a bridge between the two shapes and read the instructions up to the crew, step by step. The "mailbox," as it came to be called, worked. The carbon dioxide level fell.

Meanwhile, a different drama was underway on the ground. Ken Mattingly, the astronaut who had been bumped from the flight, worked in a simulator for hours, devising a startup sequence for Odyssey that would bring the frozen, powerless command module back to life using less electricity than a typical household appliance, and with a limited store of battery power. He tested and discarded the sequence repeatedly. Eventually he settled on one that worked. It went up to the crew as a long list of switches to flip, in a precise order.

Reentry was the final gamble. Nobody knew whether the heat shield had been damaged by the explosion. Nobody knew whether a spacecraft left to soak in the cold of space for days would restart, or whether its electronics would short out when moisture dripped on them. Before reentry, the crew jettisoned the service module, and as it drifted away they saw the damage for the first time: an entire panel of the module blown off, and a ragged wound in the side. Then they released Aquarius, which had saved them, and said goodbye to it.

On April 17, Odyssey hit the atmosphere at about 25,000 miles per hour. Reentry brings a communications blackout lasting about three minutes. This one stretched to nearly four. In Houston, nobody spoke. Then Swigert's voice came through, and the room erupted. Three parachutes bloomed over the South Pacific, and the capsule splashed down near the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima at 1:07 in the afternoon, Houston time.

The mission was officially called a successful failure. No Moon landing had taken place, but nobody had died. Congress held hearings, and NASA convened a review board that traced the accident to the tank. The agency redesigned the oxygen system, adding a third tank and removing the offending heaters and switches. Apollo went on, with more landings, until 1972.

Lovell later reflected that the crew had never seen Earth as they did on that flight: a small, blue, fragile thing, the only place they could go. They had been closer to the Moon than any humans before or since, farther from home than anyone had ever been, and the whole of it could have ended in a bang and a hiss. Instead, it ended in the Pacific, in sunlight. The people of Houston, who had worked for four days without much sleep, gave the mission a name that stuck. They called it NASA's finest hour.
